name: The Teletransportation Paradox
statement: If a machine scanned you, destroyed the original, and built an exact copy on Mars, it is unclear whether the person who steps out is you or merely a replica.
statementAccent: whether the person who steps out is you or merely a replica
meaning: The teletransportation paradox is a thought experiment about personal identity formulated by the philosopher Derek Parfit in his 1984 book Reasons and Persons. Imagine a teletransporter that puts you to sleep, records the exact molecular and atomic composition of your body and brain, destroys the original, and transmits the information to Mars, where another machine reconstructs an exact copy from new local matter, atom for atom in the same arrangement. The person who wakes on Mars has all your memories, personality, and psychology and believes they are you. The puzzle is whether that person really is you, so that you have travelled, or merely a perfect copy, so that you died on Earth and a duplicate now lives. Parfit uses the case, and a branching variant, to argue his striking conclusion that personal identity is not what matters; what matters is psychological continuity, which he calls Relation R.
mechanism: The argument turns on making identity come apart from what we care about. In the simple case one might insist the Mars person is or is not you, but Parfit sharpens the puzzle with a variant: suppose the scanner malfunctions and does not destroy the original, so there are now two people, the one on Earth and the copy on Mars, each with your memories and each equally continuous with you. They cannot both be identical to you, since they immediately diverge and are two distinct people, yet nothing about the psychological relation to your earlier self differs between the ordinary case and this one. So identity cannot be what a purely psychological duplicate preserves, and identity cannot be what fundamentally matters in survival. What matters instead is psychological continuity and connectedness, Relation R, memory, intention, personality, which the copy has in full. Parfit draws a reductionist conclusion: facts about personal identity just consist in facts about physical and psychological continuity, and once those are fixed there is no further deep fact about whether some future person is really you.

examples.text: The teletransporter records your exact composition, destroys your body, and reconstructs an atom-for-atom copy on Mars with all your memories, who believes it is you.
If the machine fails to destroy the original, there are two of you at once; since they diverge, they cannot both be you, so identity cannot be what matters.
Parfit argues what matters is psychological continuity and connectedness, memory and personality, which the copy retains, not the further question of strict identity.

variants.name: The branching or duplication case
variants.text: The version in which the original survives alongside the copy, creating two equally continuous people and showing identity can branch while continuity is preserved.

variants.name: The reductionist view of identity
variants.text: Parfit's conclusion that personal identity consists in physical and psychological continuity, with no further deep fact about whether a future person is really oneself.

whyItMatters: The teletransportation paradox is a landmark thought experiment in the metaphysics of personal identity, giving vivid form to Parfit's influential claim that identity is not what matters in survival. By showing that a purely psychological duplicate could be made, and even doubled, it pries apart identity from psychological continuity and challenges the intuition that there must be a determinate fact about whether some future person is really you. Parfit's reductionist conclusion reshaped debates about the self, survival, and what we should care about when we care about continuing to exist, with implications for ethics, prudence, and attitudes toward death. Connecting to the Ship of Theseus, brain-transplant cases, and even Buddhist ideas about the self, it remains one of the most discussed illustrations in the philosophy of personal identity.

working.text: let the machine scan and destroy you and build an exact copy elsewhere, then ask whether the copy is you or a replica of someone who died.
consider the branching case where the original survives too, producing two equally continuous people who cannot both be identical to you.
conclude with Parfit that since identity can branch, it is not what matters; psychological continuity, Relation R, is, and the copy has it.

limits: The teletransportation paradox supports Parfit's reductionist conclusion, but that conclusion is a substantive and contested position, not an established fact; many philosophers hold that identity does matter and that the Mars person either is or is not you. The argument assumes psychological continuity theories of identity and that the branching case shows identity is inessential, both of which are disputed by defenders of biological or further-fact views of the self. The scenario is also a far-fetched idealisation, and some question whether intuitions about such cases are reliable guides to the metaphysics of persons. So the experiment frames a deep debate about survival and the self rather than settling it, and Parfit's provocative thesis remains one answer among several.
misreadings: The puzzle is not merely the science-fiction question of whether teleportation would kill you; it targets what personal identity consists in and whether identity itself is what matters. Parfit's conclusion, that identity is not what matters and continuity is, is a debated philosophical position, not a proven result, so citing the paradox as showing you would definitely survive, or definitely die, overstates it. And the branching variant is not a technical quibble but the crux: it is what shows identity can come apart from the psychological continuity we actually care about, driving the reductionist argument.
origin: Formulated by the philosopher Derek Parfit in his 1984 book Reasons and Persons to probe personal identity, using the teletransporter and its branching variant to argue that identity is not what matters and that psychological continuity, Relation R, is.

sources.text: Teletransportation paradox, Wikipedia. — Parfit's 1984 formulation, the scan-destroy-reconstruct-on-Mars setup, the non-destructive branching variant, and the conclusion that psychological continuity, Relation R, is what matters.
Personal Identity, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the psychological-continuity theory, duplication thought experiments, and Parfit's view that identity itself has no practical importance.
